s: Mr. Secretary general, Mr. Vice president of the General Assembly, heads of State and government. Excellencies, ambassadors.

Ladies and gentlemen, I appear today before this assembly representing the president of the Republic of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, who has asked me to be here on his behalf and bring before you a message written by him.
From this moment on, what you will hear are the words of the president of the Republic of Colombia.
I have asked the Vice President of the Republic, José Manuel Restrepo, to read this message on my behalf.
I have done so because I assured the Colombian people that I would not leave the country during the four years of my term, and I am keeping that promise.
47 days ago, a new government took office in Colombia.
Three days later, at 7:34 a.m., the earth shook.
A 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck my country in a matter of seconds.
Homes, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges had been totally destroyed or severely damaged.
The Colombian Geological Service confirmed that this was the strongest magnitude earthquake recorded in Colombia so far this century Hundreds of Colombians lost their lives.
4500 were injured and more than 452,000 people were affected.
36,000 homes were totally destroyed.
They represented the life savings assets of these people.
The government that had barely started its work was forced to confront one of the greatest natural disasters in our recent history.
There was no time to ask whether we were ready.
We had to act, and we did so.
From the very outset.
I gave one unequivocal instruction we had to save human lives.
There was time for everything else.
Appointments to posts could wait, meetings could wait.
But my fellow fellow Colombians trapped underneath the rubble could not.
The government deployed to the affected areas alongside the security forces, emergency services, volunteers and rescue workers.
And from the very beginning, we started receiving the generous assistance from friendly countries and international organizations such as all of you.
And today, from this rostrum, I wish to express the profound and sincere gratitude of the Colombian people to all of you.
The earthquake claimed the lives of many of our fellow Colombians and destroyed thousands of homes and buildings and much infrastructure.
But it also reminded us once again of something that Colombians are very familiar with.
We might fall, we might suffer, and we might weep.
But what we cannot and what we do not know how to do is give up.
But I'm not only going to talk to you about this tragedy.
I want to refer to what Colombia decided to do in its aftermath.
On the 7th of August, I took over a country that had begun to lose something far more difficult to rebuild than a road or a building. That is trust.
merged
Trust in the law that should protect our citizens.
HUM1
Trust that working, studying, and doing things well are worthwhile.
Trust in a state that lives up to its duty.
No country, no country can prosper when its people cease to trust in it.

That's why the government that I lead has tasked itself with taking up every possible decision to enable Colombia to believe in itself again, and to ensure that the world can believe in Colombia again.
And I call that overarching purpose the patria milagro, the miracle nation.
The first step is a basic one restoring security.
PSJ1
For far too long, Colombians have had to live alongside situations that no society should accept as normal.

A rural farmer having to ask permission from a terrorist group to work on his land, a shopkeeper having to hand over part of the fruits of his labor to extortionists, a mother increasingly gripped by fear every time their child goes out to play in the park.
PSJ3
That is not, and it cannot become the norm.

Consequently, from the very beginning of my government I gave the security forces one clear instruction to regain territorial control, to fully restore the state's authority and to confront the structures using terrorism.
PSJ1
PSJ3
My government is determined to do away with euphemisms.
Organizations that murder, that kidnap, that use explosives, that recruit children, and that deliberately resort to terror to subjugate a society are terrorist groups.
INN5

Security, while essential, is not enough.
A territory that provides no opportunities remains vulnerable.
My administration is therefore also focused on ensuring that Colombia grows again.
For years, we have discussed how to better distribute what we have.
That is a legitimate, necessary discussion, but it's absolutely not enough.
We also need to ask ourselves, how are we going to produce more?
In the end?
Governments can't decree economic growth.
What they have to do is lay the foundations for it to occur.
In our miracle nation, we want an idea to be able to come, a business, a business to create jobs, and for jobs to become well-being for our people.

And it is precisely because I recognize the value of that cooperation that today I want to speak frankly about the UN.
I've been critical about this, of this organization.
I was critical of it before I became president, and it would be inconsistent to address this Assembly today and conceal my attempt to seal my convictions.
This criticism isn't born out of whim or hostility towards the United Nations.
It's based in political, institutional, doctrinal considerations.

I believe in the UN as an organization, and it is precisely for that reason that I believe it's legitimate to ask whether the institutions that we've been building are effectively responding to the problems that that it was created to address.

Allow me to begin by clarifying what I mean by that.
I'm not talking about international trade or cooperation among states, nor am I talking about a humanity that shares common problems and responsibilities.

I'm not looking to please anyone, but rather to set out the position of the Republic of Colombia respectfully, cordially and clearly.
No human institution is perfect.
All can be improved perfected, and the United Nations is no exception.
There is one specific area that Colombia wishes to reflect on further.
That is the international fight against terrorism.

This organization has done significant work here.
Since 1963, the international community has developed 19 universal legal instruments aimed at preventing different terrorist acts.
PSJ3

We need a common international definition that is sufficiently clear and precise, compatible with international law and fundamental safeguards, but also useful enough so that states can cooperate effectively in combating acts of terrorism.
PSJ3
PSJ5
A serious definition should avoid two extremes.

On the one hand, a political disagreement being arbitrarily characterized as terrorism, and on the other hand, allowing an organization to hide murders, kidnappings, bombings, or deliberate attacks against civilians behind a political label in order to evade the legal consequences of its actions.

A country that doesn't try to hide its problems, but rather to confront them.

To the nations represented here, I extend my hand respectfully and through friendship.
Colombia wants to work with you on everything that we can build together.

I want within a few years, when the world looks again at my country, I want them to see a nation that is safer, more prosperous, more well respected and above all, far more confident in its own abilities.
And if that is the Colombia that the world sees, there'll be no need to explain what I meant when I spoke of the Patria Milagro, the miracle nation.
